title: National dressing yield derived from NASS totals
notes: Ready-to-cook pounds divided by live weight pounds, both reported by NASS for the same population and period. 48,006,482 / 63,443,212 = 0.75667 for 2025. Not an estimate - it falls directly out of two measured totals.

title: Mixing pool sizes reasoned from process equipment scale
notes: Pool sizes for the mixing cascade are OUR ESTIMATES, reasoned from line speeds, chiller residence times, and standard container sizes. They are not measured. Flagged confidence=estimate throughout and shown as such in the UI. The qualitative conclusion is robust to these values: the distinct-individual curve flattens above roughly 1,000 individuals, so any plausible commodity-scale pool lands within a hair of the ceiling.

title: Mixing model parameters reasoned from grading, packing and portioning
notes:
The scalar parameters of the mixing model - how thoroughly a grader splits a pair, how many wings come up in one scoop, how much of "these two units travelled together" survives a stage - are OUR ESTIMATES, reasoned from grade-band widths, case and combo-bin sizes, and how a foodservice portion is actually taken from a bin. None of them is measured, and each is flagged confidence=estimate.
They are kept separate from project-estimate-mixing because they are a different claim. That source covers POOL SIZES - how many birds are commingled at a stage. These cover the BEHAVIOUR of a stage, which is reasoned from different evidence and can be wrong independently.
Two of them were previously bare constants in model.py, invisible to this audit. They are here so that "how much does this number matter?" is answerable from the corpus rather than from an ad-hoc sweep.

title: Placeholder pending research
notes: Explicit placeholder for stages we know exist but have not yet sourced (transport DOA, grading downgrade, cook loss). Values are deliberately wide and every one is listed in docs/RESEARCH.md open items. Anything citing this source should be treated as unverified.

title: United States Standards, Grades, and Weight Classes for Shell Eggs
notes:
Defines the defect categories and, importantly for us, the TOLERANCES - which are ceilings the pack must stay under, not measured occurrence rates. Consumer Grade AA at origin permits at most 5% checks (7% for jumbo) and at most 0.50% leakers, dirties, and loss combined, with loss itself capped at 0.30%. Grade A permits at most 7% checks (9% jumbo) and 1% combined.
Anything stored from this source is therefore an UPPER BOUND on the true rate and is flagged confidence=industry, never measured. A pack running at the tolerance would be barely passing.
Terminology: a cracked shell is a "check". Dirty or cracked eggs are "restricted" and may be diverted to an official egg products plant - a "breaker plant" - for liquid egg. They are not destroyed, but they do leave the shell-egg stream, which is what makes them a loss for the question "how many hens for a dozen eggs in a carton".

title: Confirmations of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza in Commercial and Backyard Flocks
publisher: USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service
notes: 1,689 confirmed flocks and 168.62 million birds affected between 2022 and April 2025.

title: Quarterly Agriculture Statistics 2025 Q2, Table 7: Marketing of selected animals and animal products, detailed data
notes:
The only source found that puts a head count on Israeli broilers, and a different publication from the three Statistical Abstract tables.
Chick placements, heavy breeds: 275,427,900 head for 2024 and 262,848,753 for 2023. Heavy breeds are broilers; light breeds are layers and turkeys are separate. This retires the unverified trade-press lead of "~260 million broilers/year" in docs/ISRAEL-PLAN.md - that is essentially the 2023 placement figure, now with a government citation rather than a headline whose article has since 404ed.
CBS publishes no poultry head slaughtered, in either publication. Table 7 does carry a slaughterhouse head-count block, but its 2024 total of 529,550 is exactly cattle 164,559 plus sheep and goats 229,195 plus pigs 135,796 - poultry is excluded by construction.
Annual figures are in columns Q (2024) and R (2023). The header's "P = 2011" appears to be a CBS typo or merged-cell artifact.
Also carries broiler marketing of 571,497 tonnes for 2024, which corroborates Statistical Abstract table 21.4 to within three tonnes across two separately published tables. Not loaded as a mass - see the weight basis conflict recorded on cbs-st21-11-output-2025.

title: Table 21.4, Marketing of animals and animal products by district and regional council - Statistical Abstract of Israel 2025
notes:
Broilers MARKETED in tonnes by district and regional council, 2024 only. Settles the open question at the foot of docs/ISRAEL-PLAN.md: Israel does have subnational poultry data, so a comparison against 50 US states need not be visibly lopsided.
Suppression uses "-" and ". ." exactly as NASS does, so the existing "presence, not volume" rendering applies unchanged. Six councils are suppressed and are loaded as rows with no value - never as zero.
CROSS-CHECK THAT FAILS, and it travels with either figure: the districts sum to 571,499.95 tonnes against 600,072 tonnes of output in table 21.11, a gap of 4.76%. Marketing excludes self-consumption and private sale by its own footnote 1, so the gap is probably real rather than an error -- but a reader who adds up the districts will find it, and finding it unannounced reads as a mistake in our data.
Footnote 1 also means this is "by source of product", not by place of slaughter. Footnote 3 restricts the Judea and Samaria Area row to "Israeli localities", so that row counts some of the production in that area and not all of it; it is kept with the publisher's label and the publisher's qualification rather than being renamed or dropped.
"Outside regional councils" appears once per district in the source. The bare label is not unique, so each is qualified with its district - the figure means nothing without knowing which district it is outside of.

title: Table 21.8, Livestock - Statistical Abstract of Israel 2025
notes:
Broilers in thousands, END OF YEAR, ten columns back to 1960 - the longest poultry series available for Israel, and the reason 1960-1990 figures are loaded even though nothing uses them yet.
THE TRAP ON THIS TABLE: 37,895 thousand head for 2024 is a standing flock at a point in time, not annual throughput. Broilers turn over several times a year, so reading it as slaughter understates the answer several times over. Stored as measure='inventory_eoy' so the distinction is in the data and not only in this note. It is the same inventory-versus-throughput caveat already carried on the US census sales figures.
It also neither confirms nor refutes the trade-press lead of ~260 million broilers a year in docs/ISRAEL-PLAN.md, because a flock of 37.9 million turning over five to seven times a year is consistent with it.

title: Table 21.11, Agricultural output by industry and product - Statistical Abstract of Israel 2025
notes:
Broiler output in 1,000 tonnes and value in NIS million for 2024*, 2023, 2020, 2010 and 2000. CBS's own asterisk marks 2024 provisional, and that marker is carried into the data rather than dropped.
Footnote 5 defines broilers as "Chickens intended for fattening for the meat industry", which matches our broiler species, so loading it needed no mapping decision.
What it does NOT carry, and the reason Israel cannot yet answer the count question from Israeli data: no head slaughtered, and no average bird weight anywhere in the table. "Agricultural output" is also not defined as live or dressed weight, which is why the figure is stored as measure='meat_output' in tonnes rather than mapped onto a US column that would assert one or the other.
Table eggs appear in the same table at 2,661.49 under a column headed "1,000 tonnes, unless otherwise stated". That cannot be tonnes for a country of ten million people, so it is one of the "otherwise stated" rows and is almost certainly millions of eggs. Not loaded: almost certainly is not a citation.

title: The Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) Outbreak in Poultry, 2022-Present
notes: Splits losses by sector: table-egg layers roughly 75%, turkeys 11%, BROILERS only about 8%. Broiler farms hold fewer birds, are restocked faster, and the birds live ~47 days so cumulative exposure is far lower. This is the key finding for our purposes - HPAI is overwhelmingly an egg story, not a wing story.

title: Food waste reduction in commercial kitchens (Winnow, EPA materials)
notes: Food waste typically runs 4% to 13% of food costs in commercial kitchens. Spoilage specifically ranges 1-5% in prepare-ahead operations and 1-6% in cook-to-order operations. Corroborates the ReFED band.

title: Fees paid to growers for raising broiler chickens varied widely in 2020
notes: Grower pay clusters at 3.8 to 4.6 cents per pound of live weight, set by a relative "tournament" system in which each farm's rate depends on its performance against others delivering in the same period.

title: Supermarket Loss Estimates for Fresh Fruit, Vegetables, Meat, Poultry, and Seafood and Their Use in the ERS Loss-Adjusted Food Availability Data
notes: Retail-level shrink. ERS previously assumed a flat 7% retail loss for every meat, poultry, and seafood category; this study replaced that with measured supermarket estimates, cutting loss-adjusted fresh meat, poultry, and seafood availability by 7.3% for 2012.

title: Maximum Line Speed Rates for Young Chicken and Turkey Establishments Operating Under the New Poultry Inspection System
publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service / Federal Register
notes:
Plants under the New Poultry Inspection System may run 175 birds per minute; everyone else is capped at 140. 47 plants held waivers as of 2018. FSIS proposed formalising 175 bpm in February 2026.
Directly relevant to wing damage: comment records attribute improperly hung shackles, insufficient bleeding, and scalding of live birds to faster lines - shackling being the exact mechanism behind broken wings. FSIS counters that waiver plants meet or exceed food safety standards. Note that food safety and carcass DAMAGE are different questions; the FSIS defence addresses the former, not the latter.

title: Food Standards and Labeling Policy Book
publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
notes: "Wings" is a REGULATED term. A product labelled wings must be the entire wing with all muscle and skin intact, except that the tip may be removed. Where bone has been removed the name must say so. Also defines the solid-muscle / chunked-and-formed / ground-and-formed distinction that separates a whole-muscle boneless wing from a reformed nugget.

title: Census of Agriculture 2022, broiler data by state
notes:
The census breaks the suppression ceiling. NASS's annual SURVEY programme withholds states with too few operations - the same 22-state cap applies in the QuickStats API as in the PDFs, which was confirmed directly by querying it. The CENSUS is a separate five-yearly enumeration with different disclosure handling, and for broilers at state level it publishes ALL 50 STATES with nothing withheld.
California is the clearest illustration: 313.7 million broilers sold in 2022, eighth largest in the country, and absent from every year of both annual publications.
Caveat carried deliberately: these are SALES in a census year, not slaughter or production, and they do not move until the 2027 census. They answer "which states raise broilers and at what scale" - never mix them into an annual time series.

title: Chickens and Eggs 2025 Summary
notes:
The anchor for everything egg. Annual estimates cover December 1 of the previous year through November 30, which is NOT a calendar year - do not align it with the slaughter summary's calendar-year series.
US 2025: layers averaged 365 million, annual production per layer on hand 288 eggs, total production 105 billion eggs (90.1 billion table, 15.2 billion hatching).
Internally consistent to a degree worth noting: average layers times eggs per layer reproduces reported total production for all 31 states with 2025 figures, zero mismatches beyond 1%. And 288 eggs/year divided by 365 days gives 0.789 eggs/hen/day, which independently matches the 78.7-79.9 eggs per 100 layers per day reported in the monthly releases. Two unrelated tables agreeing is the strongest validation in the project.
Coverage is BETTER than broilers: 34 states named across 2024-2025 against 23 for slaughter. Maryland, South Dakota, and Virginia are suppressed for 2025 but present for 2024.

title: Chickens and Eggs, monthly releases 2026
notes:
Monthly rate of lay and layer inventory. Rate of lay per day ran 79.1 (Jan 1), 78.9 (Feb 1), 79.9 (May 1), and 78.7 (Jun 1) eggs per 100 layers in 2026 - remarkably steady. June 1 2026 layer inventory 377 million total: 312 million table-egg, 60.7 million broiler-type hatching, 4.70 million egg-type hatching.
The table-egg versus hatching split matters for us: they are different birds with very different lay rates, and a state's headline eggs-per-layer figure is largely a readout of which mix it runs.

title: Poultry Slaughter 2025 Summary
notes: Definitive US slaughter statistics. NASS reports the broiler population under the category "Young Chickens", defined in the report as "commercially grown broilers-fryers and other young immature birds such as roasters and capons". Highest-confidence source in the project.

title: Poultry - Production and Value 2025 Summary
notes:
Broilers PRODUCED by state - head, live weight, and value - over December 1 to November 30. A different publication and a different population from the Poultry Slaughter summary, which counts young chickens SLAUGHTERED per calendar year and also includes roasters and capons. 2025: 9.40 billion produced against 9.58 billion slaughtered. The two must never be summed or treated as one series.
Carried for two reasons. First, it independently CONFIRMS our state live weights: production pounds divided by head reproduces the slaughter report's state average for all 14 states the 2025 table names, exactly, from a separate survey. Second, it RECOVERS STATES - NASS suppresses different states in different years and publications, and Florida is individually reported here for 2024 while appearing in no year of the slaughter summary.

title: Egg, whole, raw, fresh (FDC 171287)
notes:
Per 100 g of edible contents: 143 kcal, 12.56 g protein, 9.51 g fat, 372 mg cholesterol. A US large egg is about 50 g of contents, so roughly 72 kcal and 6.3 g protein each.
Only a raw row is carried. A wing has one dominant preparation - breaded and deep fried - which makes raw-versus-fried an informative pair. An egg has no canonical preparation, and scrambling in butter changes the numbers because of the butter. Storing one arbitrary cooked row would assert a default that does not exist.

title: Fast foods, fried chicken, wing, meat and skin and breading (FDC 170360)
notes: Breaded and fried. Roughly 59% of calories from fat against 27% from protein - the breading and frying oil, not the bird, drive the change.

title: Chicken, broilers or fryers, wing, meat and skin, raw (FDC 172390)
notes: Per 100 g: 191 kcal, 17.5 g protein, 12.8 g fat. The reference figure for an unbreaded, uncooked whole wing with skin.

title: Production, Supply and Distribution database, Israel broiler meat production, market years 1964-2000
notes:
Held ONLY as evidence in the CBS weight-basis question. No figure from it is loaded, and it is not an Israeli source.
The question it addresses: CBS reports Israeli broiler tonnage but never states whether the figure is live weight or carcass weight, so the tonnage cannot be used for anything that depends on the basis. USDA PSD reports broiler meat on a ready-to-cook basis by its own convention, which makes it a yardstick.
The one overlapping year is 2000. CBS reports 270,000 tonnes; PSD reports 195,000 tonnes. The ratio is 72.2%, which is dressing-yield shaped - this project's own US figure derives to 75.67% from two NASS totals. If CBS were already reporting carcass weight the ratio would sit near 100%.
That is evidence for CBS being LIVE weight, not proof, and three things keep it from being proof. It is a single overlapping year. That year is 2000, twenty-six years before the figures actually in use. And PSD's unit string for broiler meat is a bare "(1000 MT)" where its beef series says "(1000 MT CWE)" explicitly, so the ready-to-cook basis is convention rather than a label on the row.
Two further checks, both consistent with live weight and neither decisive. CBS's own output and marketing series agree at 95-100% for the same year, so both share one basis and the gap between them is stock change rather than dressing. And 571,497 tonnes marketed against 275,427,900 chicks placed gives 2.075 kg per bird placed, or about 2.18 kg per bird marketed at 5% farm mortality - plausible as a live weight for Israel's smaller birds, and requiring roughly 2.9 kg live if read as carcass weight.
Recorded as a conflict rather than resolved, per the rule in docs/research/README.md that a source disagreement is reported and not adjudicated, and because promoting this to a stated basis is a human judgement about provenance.

title: Fully Cooked Breaded Whole Muscle Boneless Chicken Wings, product specs
notes: Manufacturer piece weights for commercial boneless wings: 0.76 oz and 0.79 oz per finished breaded piece. A 3.78 oz portion is about six pieces. Note the product category name Tyson itself uses - "boneless wings & chunks" - and the descriptor "whole muscle chicken breast". These are breast chunks, and the manufacturer does not pretend otherwise.

title: Boneless wings and chunks product line, ingredient statements
notes: Ingredient statements across the line read "boneless, skinless chicken BREAST chunks with rib meat". Rib meat is the portion left attached to the breast during deboning - part of the front quarter, NOT the wing. So "chunks" contain no wing meat either, and the phrase "with rib meat" is a breast-yield allowance rather than a different cut sneaking in.

title: A method of production of boneless chicken wings (drumettes and winglets) by separation of periosteum from bone without cutting skin and muscles
notes: Segment masses: bone-in drumette 39.9 g at 74.9% boneless yield, bone-in winglet 30.7 g at 80.1% boneless yield.

title: Moisture retention by water- and air-chilled broilers, and effect of immersion or dry air chilling on carcass moisture retention
notes:
Air chilling LOSES 2.5-2.84% of prechill weight; immersion chilling GAINS 4.14% in one study and 9.3% in another, with a range of 3.4-14.7%. Overall carcass yield: immersion +6.5%, combination inline air +1.98%, air chill -1.10%.
This is a MASS effect only. Chilling method changes what a wing weighs by up to a tenth; it cannot change how many wings a chicken has. It therefore belongs in the mass stages and can never move a count answer - but it matters a great deal to anyone buying wings by the pound.

title: The impact of refrigeration on food losses and associated greenhouse gas emissions throughout the supply chain
notes: Models food loss across 10 supply chain stages and finds improved refrigeration cuts losses 26-63% for meat, milk, and produce. IMPORTANTLY it does NOT break out a transport-stage loss rate, and the authors state that underlying food loss rate data "remain uncertain". Cited here as evidence that a clean transit figure does not exist, not as a source for one. For meat the paper finds post-harvest handling and storage, not transport, is where refrigeration matters most.

title: The Japanese Wagyu beef industry: current situation and future prospects -- A review
notes:
Gotoh, Nishimura, Kuchida & Mannen (2018). Peer-reviewed, but COOPER may not assign `study` -- the figure below is graded `industry` by human decision, same rule as every other peer-reviewed source in this project (see the honey batch's Jaganathan & Mandal lesson in docs/research/README.md).
A single source that carried four of batch-03-wagyu's six items in principle (carcass/finishing weights, the yield/quality/BMS grading structure, days on feed, total feed consumption) -- extraction still returned only one figure from it. See docs/research/accepted/batch-03-wagyu-REVIEW.md for why: the model mostly declined to return a candidate at all against a document that demonstrably contained the answers, a different failure shape than vanilla's wrong-question/gate-limit drops.
The PMC mirror (PMC6039323) returned a reCAPTCHA wall on 2026-08-15; fetched here from the publisher (animbiosci.org) instead.
Round 2 (2026-08-16, human read of the same fetched document) recovered two more figures from it: the Japanese Black carcass-yield weights (756 kg live / 476 kg carcass at 29.2 months) and the JMGA grading structure (yield letter A-C, quality number 1-5, BMS 1-12 as one of four inputs to the quality number). See docs/research/accepted/batch-03-wagyu-REVIEW-round2.md.

title: Prevalence of breast muscle myopathies (spaghetti meat, woody breast, white striping) and associated risk factors in broiler chickens
notes: White striping 96.0%, spaghetti meat 36.3%, severe woody breast 11.8%. 85.1% of fillets showed more than one myopathy. Risk rises with live weight, so big-bird deboning flocks - precisely the birds boneless product comes from - are the worst affected. Woody breast incidence rose from about 5% in 2012 to 29% by 2015.

title: Broiler Production System Life Cycle Assessment: 2020 Update
publisher: National Chicken Council / University of Arkansas
notes: Full ReCiPe lifecycle assessment built on Agri-Stats national data. Reference flow is one broiler at 6.37 lb live weight. Per average bird in 2020: 2.90 kg CO2 eq, 5.26 m2a crop eq land, 0.73 m3 water, 0.61 kg oil eq fossil resources, 5.87 g PM2.5 eq. Per kg live weight: 1.00, 1.85, 0.25, 0.21, 2.03 respectively. Improvements 2010-2020: global warming -18.1%, land -13.0%, water -13.0%, fossil -22.1%, PM -13.8%. Also gives 1.053 baby chicks per broiler produced to cover mortality, which independently corroborates our farm_mortality stage.

title: Escherichia coli O157:H7 in Ground Beef - Review of a Draft Risk Assessment
publisher: National Research Council / Institute of Medicine, National Academies Press
notes:
The structure of a ground beef lot, on a host the pipeline can actually reach. "Trim is removed from each carcass and combined into 2,000-pound combo bins during the slaughter process." "Grinder loads are presumed to vary in size from the equivalent of 2 to 15 combo bins of trim." And, in the Slaughter Module chapter (NBK221092): "Lot is defined in the draft as the number of cattle necessary to fill one combo bin with trim; and a single lot may take one or more truckloads of cattle."
HOW IT WAS FOUND, because the method generalises. The figures wanted here live in an FSIS draft risk assessment, and fsis.usda.gov returns HTTP 403 to this project's fetcher site-wide - verified against three paths on two separate days. This volume is the National Academies REVIEWING that draft, and it quotes the definitions at length. When an agency document is unfetchable, look for the body that reviewed it: oversight literature quotes what it reviews, and oversight publishers host differently.
Note "presumed" in the grinder-load sentence. It is a modelling assumption inside a risk assessment, not an observation, which is why the combo-bin pool derived from it is graded `estimate`.

title: Estimating Animal Abundance in Ground Beef Batches Assayed with Molecular Markers
publisher: Hu X-S, Simila J, Platz SS, Moore SS, Plastow G, Meghen CN; PLoS ONE 7(3):e34191
notes:
The most important source in the ground beef subject and the only measured mixing pool anywhere in this corpus. DNA markers profiled in six commercial grind batches, animal abundance estimated by mark-recapture: "An average of 411 to1367 animals was present in the six grind batches." (The missing space is the document's own.)
Promoted to `study` by hand. COOPER graded it `industry` because it cannot grade higher, and the promotion rests on a narrow point that the honey batch taught: 411-1,367 is this paper's own primary result, not uncited scene-setting borrowed from someone else. The same paper's "a single ground beef batch may consist of many hundreds of animals" IS scene-setting, and is deliberately not used as a figure anywhere.
Four things it is not, all easy to get wrong: not a per-patty count (a batch is many bins); not a per-bin count; not a national figure (six batches, one manufacturer, one line, one shift); and not a mean worth quoting on its own - the paper's own point is the variance between batches.

title: Multi-silkworm cocoon: structure, properties and the collective spinning behaviour behind it (Int J Biol Macromol, PMID 38061509)
notes:
Cited for ONE sentence and graded deliberately below what its source_type would suggest: "A normal silkworm cocoon (NSC) with a unique nonwoven structure is usually spun by a single silkworm larva."
THE PAPER IS PEER-REVIEWED AND THAT SENTENCE IS NOT ITS FINDING. It is uncited scene-setting in a materials-science study about cocoon structure, so the figure it supports is graded `industry`, not `study`. This is exactly the distinction the research README draws using Jaganathan & Mandal on honey, and it is the reason `study` is a human-only grade: a model that sees a journal header cannot tell a paper's result from its first sentence.
Cited because it is the ONLY fetchable source found, across a 35-URL sweep covering FAO, Britannica, Wikipedia, Saint Louis Zoo, Carolina Biological and several extension PDFs, that states the one-cocoon-per-silkworm relation in a single sentence at all. Sericulture writers treat it as too obvious to count and write "the larvae enclose themselves in a cocoon", which contains no number and cannot ground a figure of 1.
It also supplies its own exception, which is kept rather than trimmed: three or more larvae sometimes spin one cocoon collectively in a particular Bombyx mori genetic resource. So the constant is one-to-one for commercial silk and is not a law of nature.

title: The Influence of Welfare Training on Bird Welfare and Carcass Quality in Two Commercial Poultry Primary Processing Plants
notes: 90% of bruising occurs in the 12-24 hours before processing. Bruise distribution by region: breast 42%, wings 33%, legs 25%.

title: Rearing and handling injuries in broiler chickens and risk factors for wing injuries during loading
notes: Median wing injuries per load 5.7%, against under 1% per load for legs, breast, and shoulders. Wings are by a wide margin the most damaged part of the bird. Load-to-load variance is high, so this is stored with a wide lo/hi band.

title: Yield of Carcass, Parts, Meat, Skin, and Bone of Eight Strains of Broilers
notes: Whole wing as a share of carcass weight (9.1-10.2%) and of live weight (6.7-7.3%), measured across eight commercial broiler strains.

title: Fact Sheet: Beef Grading (Expected Yields of Closely Trimmed, Boneless Retail Cuts by USDA Yield Grade)
publisher: National Cattlemen's Beef Association / beefresearch.org (Cattlemen's Beef Board checkoff)
notes: Checkoff-funded fact sheet authored by Daryl Tatum PhD (Colorado State), citing the 1996 USDA grading standard directly. Cited for the %CTBRC column of its Table 1: closely trimmed boneless retail cuts from round/loin/rib/chuck ONLY, <45.4% to >52.3% of carcass weight across USDA Yield Grades 5 through 1. The companion %Total Yield column (all retail cuts including ground beef, <65 to >=80) is a different denominator and is not interchangeable with it -- nor with SDSU's 65% worked-example figure, which includes trim the %CTBRC basis excludes.

title: Beef Grades and Carcass Information
notes:
A DIFFERENT MSU Extension publication from msstate-ext-beef-yield (farm-direct beef), despite the same publisher and overlapping subject. This one is the grading fact sheet, cited for the fed-cattle dressing percentage: "It typically ranges from 60 to 64 percent for the majority of fed cattle and averaged 64 percent for the Mississippi Farm to Feedlot program cattle from 1993 through 2007." Same 60-64 range the other MSU document states, independently restated with a measured program mean attached -- consistent, and not merged into one citation because they are two documents.
Also the document that treats marbling/quality-grade and fat-thickness/yield-grade as independently measured traits throughout, which is the basis for batch-03-wagyu's honest marbling_vs_yield_tradeoff "sources treat the axes as independent" finding.

title: How Much Meat to Expect from a Beef Animal (farm-direct beef)
notes:
"The average dressing percentage of beef cattle is 60 to 64 percent." Cited for dressing, and for the upper bound of the carcass-to-packaged band.
Carries a conflict this project records rather than resolves. Its take-home sentence gives two figures that do not reconcile with each other: "the take-home weight of packaged beef will be approximately 40 percent of the animal's live weight, or 75 percent of the hot carcass weight." At its own 63 percent dressing percent, 75 percent of the carcass is 47 percent of live weight, not 40. SDSU's 65 percent does reconcile. Both bounds are kept and neither is averaged away.

title: U.S. Broiler Performance
notes: Year-by-year series of market age, market weight, feed conversion, and grow-out mortality going back to 1925. Trade body rather than government, so figures are tagged confidence=industry.

title: Broiler Chicken Industry Key Facts
notes: Industry structure - plant counts, company counts, contract farms.

title: How Much Sap Can One Tree Produce?
publisher: New York State Maple Producers Association
notes:
A producers' association page, and the most quotable of the three - which is exactly why it needs watching. It supplies the modal "most trees today have only one tap", which is load-bearing here: it is what lets a per-TAP yield stand in for a per-TREE yield without inventing a multiplier.
It also states the bare "approximately 40 gallons of sap" that COOPER preferred over UVM's rule. Kept as a source because the one-tap figure is genuinely useful, cited for the ratio nowhere.

title: ענף הלול - סיכום 2021 (Poultry sector summary, 2021)
publisher: ארגון מגדלי עופות בישראל (Israel Poultry Growers Organisation)
notes:
The growers' organisation, not the statutory Poultry Board - note the domains, ofot.CO.il is the growers and ofot.ORG.il is the council. Undated on the page beyond the year it summarises, so published_on is NULL.
Carries a sector table for 2021 that no government publication matches: 3,630 active growers across family farms and kibbutzim, of which 604 raise broilers producing 515,400 tonnes worth NIS 3,414 million, 2,863 produce 2,230 million table eggs, and 78 breeding operations supply 244 million chicks.
HOW THIS DOCUMENT WAS FOUND is worth recording. COOPER fetched it during batch-05 and both models returned nothing from it; a human reading the same downloaded file found the table in minutes. That is the second time the returned artifacts have been worth more than the extraction, and it is the reason raw documents come back with every batch. See docs/research/accepted/batch-05-israel-hebrew-REVIEW.md.
Graded 'trade_body' rather than 'government': it is an industry association reporting on its own members. Nobody enumerated these figures the way NASS enumerates US slaughter, and the corpus should not imply otherwise by placing them in the same tier.

title: Shechita: All About Kosher Ritual Slaughter
notes:
A kosher certification agency describing its own procedure, which makes it authoritative on WHAT HAPPENS and silent on HOW OFTEN.
For poultry, post-slaughter bedikah inspects the lungs, intestines and tendon junctions, and a mashgiach pulls any bird with a blemish off the line for a rav to rule on. That is a loss stage with no US analogue - FSIS has no equivalent check - and it should push the birds-required number up.
NO REJECTION RATE IS PUBLISHED, here or anywhere reachable. So the stage can be described honestly and cannot yet be quantified: any figure we put on it would be an 'estimate' of our own making, which is the grade the project is trying to reduce. Recorded as a known gap rather than filled.

title: Saffron: A Tale of Red Gold and How to Produce Your Own
notes:
Held for its per-acre yield figure, which CONFLICTS with HS661 and is stored as a conflict rather than reconciled: Penn State says "one acre of land produces only about 3 pounds", HS661 says "an annual yield of 8-10 pounds of dried saffron per acre is obtained in an established planting".
Both are plausible and they are probably not measuring the same thing - HS661 explicitly says "in an established planting", and a saffron field takes years to reach that state. Neither figure is loaded as data. The disagreement is recorded because a three-fold spread between two extension services is the most honest thing we know about saffron yields.
Also states "It takes about 50 flowers to produce just one teaspoon of dried saffron", which is consistent with 150 flowers per gram only if a teaspoon of threads is about a third of a gram. Not loaded: converting it would require assuming the mass of a teaspoon of saffron, and that assumption would be ours rather than the source's.

title: Foodservice methodology, Insights Engine Food Waste Monitor
notes: Restaurants and foodservice generated 12.5 million tons of surplus food in 2024. Pre-consumer waste - spoilage, over-ordering, overproduction - runs 4% to 10% of food purchased. Separately, roughly 4.2% of food purchases go unutilised in commercial kitchens on average across Leanpath's client base. Post-consumer plate waste is about 70% of total foodservice waste but is deliberately EXCLUDED from this model: those wings reached the plate, which is where our question stops.

title: How Much Meat Can You Expect from a Fed Steer?
notes:
The ground-beef-specific yield, which is the figure the subject actually needs: "This 150 -185 pounds of lean trim would likely be packaged as ground beef." The space before the dash is the page's own typography and is preserved everywhere it is quoted - tidying it is what made a true quote fail the gate on the Wikipedia row in this same batch.
Also carries the whole-chain arithmetic that reconciles: a 1,200 lb steer at 63 percent dressing gives a 750 lb carcass, "about 65% of the carcass weight, or roughly 490 pounds, as boneless, trimmed beef", which is "approximately 40% of the live weight". That internal consistency is why the 65 percent figure anchors the low end of the carcass-to-packaged band while MSU's 75 percent anchors the high end.
Lean trim is roughly a third of total packaged beef. The two must never be merged; only the trim figure becomes patties.

title: Saffron - Garden Help, Herbs
publisher: UC Master Gardeners of Santa Clara County, UC ANR
notes:
Undated, which is why published_on is NULL rather than guessed.
The load-bearing source for flowers-per-gram: "Each plant typically produces 2 to 4 flowers, and approximately 150 flowers are needed to yield 1 gram of dried spice." It also states three stigmas per flower independently of HS661, which is why that constant is treated as settled.
This document was fetched by COOPER and then NOT extracted from - the retrieval stage found it, the extraction stage read only the HS661 PDF. The figure was recovered by a human reading the returned artifact. That is a pipeline finding, not a data one, and it is recorded here because it is the reason the raw documents come back with every batch.

title: Saffron - Crocus sativus L. (HS661)
publisher: University of Florida IFAS Extension, Horticultural Sciences
notes:
James M. Stephens, professor emeritus. Original publication May 1994, revised September 2015, reviewed October 2018 - so the figures are old, and saffron husbandry has not changed much in thirty years or three thousand.
Fetched as a PDF reprint by COOPER during batch-01-saffron. Worth recording that the PDF was nearly missed: the pdftotext path failed and only the pypdf fallback recovered it, which is why that fallback exists.
Carries two figures used here: three stigmas per blossom, and 210,000 stigmas per pound of saffron. The second is hedged in the source's own words ("Supposedly"), and it is stored at confidence=industry for exactly that reason.

title: Bulletin #7036: How to Tap Maple Trees and Make Maple Syrup
notes:
Source for taps-per-tree by trunk diameter and for the conservative end of the per-tap seasonal yield. Its tapping guidance is stricter than older literature - one tap below 18 inches, a second only at 18 to 25 inches, a third only on very healthy trees over 25 inches - which is the direction the whole industry has moved for tree health.
Its season is given as calendar windows rather than a duration ("mid-February to early April in Southern Maine"), which is why season_length came back from COOPER with a quote and no number. That was the correct behaviour: subtracting two dates would have been our arithmetic, not the source's.

title: Chinese appetite for chicken paws proves a boon for U.S. producers
notes: Chicken paws and wing tips together form roughly a $648 million annual US export market, sold into China for soups, stews, and snacking. Rendering the same volume domestically would return less than a tenth of that. Paws fetch $0.80-$1.00/lb exported against $0.05-$0.10/lb as domestic animal feed - close to a tenfold difference.

title: The "Jones Rule of 86" Revisited
publisher: University of Vermont Extension, Proctor Maple Research Center
notes:
The strongest maple source in the corpus and the only one that gives a RULE rather than a constant: divide 86 by the sap sugar concentration in degrees Brix to get gallons of sap per gallon of syrup. Devised by C.H. Jones at UVM in 1946.
Preferred over the folk "40 gallons" wherever both would serve, because 40:1 is only true near 2 Brix and this document says so in the same breath: an average 2 Brix sap "would require 43 gallons of sap to produce 1 gallon of syrup, or a sap:syrup ratio of close to 40:1".
Worth recording that COOPER read this document and quoted the weaker source anyway in batch-07-maple. The passage was retrieved and in front of the model - a single chunk, returned by best_chunks - so the preference for the round number was the model's, not a retrieval failure. See docs/research/accepted/batch-07-maple-REVIEW.md.
Also note the document's own caveat: the rule degrades at the high sugar concentrations reverse osmosis now produces, so it is a field rule, not a physical law.

title: Package of Practice: Vanilla Cultivation
publisher: North Eastern Council (NEC) / North Eastern Development Finance Corporation Limited (NEDFi), India
notes:
Undated within the document itself; the URL path carries a 2021 upload date, kept out of published_on since it names the upload, not necessarily authorship. A regional development-finance body's model project profile for vanilla cultivation, in the same "extension-style practical guide" category as Penn State's and UF/IFAS's saffron sources.
Sole source for the only figure batch-02-vanilla accepted: green_to_cured_ratio, "About 6 kg of green pods produce 1 kg of cured beans." Confirmed to state Vanilla planifolia by name.

title: Guide on Sustainable Vanilla Cultivation
notes: 4,433 lines after pdftotext. Strong on pollination and field yields (43 and 48 keyword hits respectively) but mentions "cured" exactly once, so it could not answer the curing ratio -- coverage was checked per source before batch-02-vanilla was sent, not assumed. Also the source for the dropped flowers_per_bean row's quote ("A flower gives a vanilla bean after hand pollination") -- true, and never loaded as data, because the numeral 1 never appears in that sentence. See docs/research/accepted/batch-02-vanilla-REVIEW.md.

title: Overcoming challenges in refrigerated transport
notes: Qualitative. Identifies the loss mechanisms for meat in transit - temperature excursion triggering load rejection at the receiving dock, physical damage, and mishandling - and notes temperature abuse during LOADING causes more rejected shipments than transit failures. No quantified rejection rate is given, in this or any source found.

title: Broken Eggs 101: A Practical Guide for Commercial Egg Buyers and Sellers
notes:
In-transit breakage expectations from the buy side. Commercial buyers expect under 1% for Grade A shell eggs; well-run short hauls come in under 0.5%; long hauls and export run 1.5-2% without optimised handling.
Trade press rather than a measured study, so confidence=industry. Carried because it is the only quantified transit figure found for eggs, and the contrast with wings is instructive: frozen IQF wings are robust enough that no citable transit figure exists at all, while eggs are fragile enough that the industry measures breakage closely - it is what the invoice argument is about.

title: Going up in smoke, Sabra style
notes:
Held for one specific thing: it names what actually goes on the mangal for Yom Ha'atzmaut, and chicken wings are on that list alongside pargiyot - deboned chicken thighs, cubed and skewered - with the meal built around small cuts and many salads rather than large joints.
That makes this project's exact product part of an Israeli national holiday, which is a better demo hook than any production statistic. It also observes that falafel, shawarma and schnitzel - the dishes outsiders name first - play very little role in the day.
Undated on the page, so published_on is NULL rather than guessed.

title: The Grilling Tradition of Israel's Independence Day
notes: Independent corroboration that Yom Ha'atzmaut grilling is near-universal rather than a niche custom - the mangal treated as as essential to the day as the president's speech - and that the tradition, while imported, has become distinctly Israeli. Two sources agreeing is why the cultural fact is loaded at all.

title: Carcass Grading (breeding guide technical resources)
notes:
Commercial source -- an American wagyu breeder, not JMGA or a peer-reviewed paper -- graded industry accordingly. Cited ONLY for the BMS-to-quality-grade bucketing (BMS 8-12 -> quality 5; BMS 5-7 -> 4) and its "a BMS 3 grade requires a minimum of 21% IMF" anchor, plus the ribbing-site basis note (Japan ribs between the 6th/7th rib, the US between the 12th/13th).
NOT usable as a definition of what BMS measures: Fable's adversarial review (2026-08-16) confirmed this page attributes color, firmness and texture to the BMS grade itself, but per Gotoh BMS is a marbling-only score -- the four-factor lowest-of rule belongs to the separate meat quality grade (1-5). See docs/research/accepted/batch-03-wagyu-findings-round2.yaml.

title: Silkworm
notes:
A tertiary reference work - an encyclopedia entry, not a survey and not a study. Graded and cited as what it is.
Carried because it is the only silk source we hold that names a primary reference for its central figure: the cocoons-per-pound claim is attributed to Palmer 1949, which we have NOT seen. The citation in this corpus is therefore to the encyclopedia that carries the number, not to Palmer, on the principle that citing a paper through a source you have read is how a rumour acquires a footnote.
It is also the source of the sourced filament length, 300-900 m, which sits well below the commonly repeated "1,000-1,600 m". The lower sourced figure is the one to keep; the folk range has no source we could find.

title: Contract Broiler Production: Questions and Answers
notes: A 20,000 sq ft house grosses roughly $34,000-$40,000 a year at average performance against $28,000-$30,000 of fixed and cash costs, leaving $6,000-$12,000 to the grower's land, labour, and management during the 15-year mortgage period.

title: Israel poultry industry hit by war and labour shortage
notes:
By Vladislav Vorotnikov. Explains a hole that is already visible in our CBS series: 16 million head of poultry lost across Newcastle disease outbreaks in Q4 2023, on top of poultry houses shut in the north and south and a labour shortage after foreign workers left. CBS output for 2023 is 553,068 tonnes - below 2020 - and this is why.
NOTE ON REACHABILITY: this URL returns 403 to some automated fetchers and 200 to an ordinary browser user-agent. It is alive; a 403 here is a bot filter, not a dead link. Do not retire it on one failed fetch.
Two figures in it are THIRD-HAND and are deliberately not loaded as data: Of HaGalil at about 15% of Israeli chicken slaughter and Of Oz at about 5%. Poultry World is citing TheMarker, which is citing unnamed industry sources. Worth knowing that both named plants sit in places our own district data covers - Kiryat Shmona in the north, Sha'ar HaNegev in the south, the latter marketing 9,813 tonnes of broilers in 2024 - so the claim is checkable in principle against a Hebrew original.

title: The Silk Road - Connecting Peoples and Cultures
publisher: Smithsonian Center for Folklife and Cultural Heritage
notes:
A museum festival programme essay. The best provenance available for a cocoons-per-necktie figure, which says more about the state of that figure than about the Smithsonian.
It gives 150 cocoons per necktie. Two other figures circulate - 120-130 at AFB Education, and 110 across several retail and content-farm pages, all reproducing one unattributed sentence verbatim. This source is preferred on provenance alone, NOT on any evidence it is more accurate, and the conflict is recorded on the product row rather than resolved. No survey exists behind any of the three.
It replaced bows-n-ties, which carries the 120-130 figure in a browser and serves an article body that JavaScript truncates mid-word. To the project's fetcher that page contains neither 120 nor 130, so two research runs correctly returned nothing and read as model weakness for a week.

title: Silk Thread and Cloth
notes:
A schoolteacher's silkworm-rearing page for classroom use. The weakest provenance of anything cited in this corpus, and it is cited anyway for two figures because no better source states them and pretending otherwise would be worse than saying so plainly.
What it is good for: the FIVE-cocoons-per-thread reeling figure, which is the only mixing pool size in the entire project backed by a citation rather than by our own estimate. Both COOPER models returned it independently.
What to watch: its per-garment sentence answers two questions at once - "It takes 1700 to 2000 cocoons to make one silk dress (or about 1,000 cocoons for a silk shirt)." A previous research run stored the DRESS numbers in the SHIRT row and passed every automatic check, because every figure involved genuinely appears in the quote. Anyone re-reading this source should read the clause, not the sentence.
Historical footnote: this page is also where the entity-decoding bug was found. It carries 47 non-breaking spaces, and until fetch_url() learned to call html.unescape() they survived into the inbox and made an honest quote from it impossible to verify.

title: Poultry producers warn first-ever imports of chickens will destroy local farms
notes:
By Sue Surkes. The most useful Israeli poultry source found outside CBS, and the only one carrying the figure CBS does not publish: roughly 260 million broilers raised a year.
Attribution matters here and is the reason this is usable at all. The figures are attributed to a NAMED industry official - Moti Elkabetz, secretary of the Poultry Breeders Association - rather than to "sources" or "industry estimates". That makes it an industry figure with a person behind it, not an anonymous claim.
Also carries: NIS 10 billion annual turnover, about 600 large chicken farms, 20 kosher poultry slaughterhouses, some 6,000 dependent jobs, a 40-day grow-out, about 30% of product sold frozen, NIS 6.5/kg paid to the farmer against about NIS 20/kg at retail.
The 58.2 kg per-capita figure it quotes is sourced to Euromeatnews, whose article now 404s, so that number is NOT loaded from here. A live article citing a dead one does not resurrect the citation.
